newsitem.title: USA: Clinton urges both sides in Israel not to provoke.
newsitem.headline: Clinton urges both sides in Israel not to provoke.

text.p: President Bill Clinton on Thursday urged Israelis and Palestinians to end the bloodshed in the Arab territories and not take "unnecessarily provocative actions" that exacerbate tensions.

With a rising death toll from two days of clashes between Palestinians and Israelis in the West Bank and Gaza Strip, Clinton and his top officials engaged in frantic diplomatic efforts to try to salvage the Middle East peace process.
Clinton stopped short of calling Israel's opening of a tourist tunnel near Moslem holy sites in east Jerusalem a provocation but made clear Washington felt it was an irritant to the peace process.

Addressing both Israelis and Palestinians, he said: "Our message to them is this: It is in everyone's interest to resolve their differences peacefully, to work together on security and to avoid any actions that could make progress on the peace between Israelis and Palestinians more difficult."

Asked if Israel should seal up the tunnel, he said: "What I think is they need to end the violence and they need to discuss these matters between them and they need to ask themselves, all of them do, what can we do to avoid unnecessarily provocative actions."
White House spokesman Mike McCurry told reporters "the parties should take no steps that raise new issues" and he said the tunnel "is clearly a new issue."

Arab anger at Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's failure to extend self-rule in the West Bank and Gaza boiled over on Wednesday when his right-wing government opened an archaeological tunnel near Moslem holy places.

Israeli troops killed 33 Palestinians and PLO police shot dead 10 Israelis in gun battles and stone-throwing clashes on Thursday, the bloodiest day in the West Bank and Gaza since Yasser Arafat set up his self-rule Palestinian government.
The fierce fighting shook U.S. hopes of keeping alive Arab-Israeli peace talks, stalled since Netanyahu came to power 100 days ago.

Secretary of State Warren Christopher, in New York at the U.N. General Assembly, spoke to Netanyahu by phone on Wednesday and State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said they were expected to talk again later. Burns said Christopher also planned to talk to Arafat.
U.S. Middle East coordinator Dennis Ross has been on the phone almost continously to Arafat, other Palestinians and Netanyahu adviser Dore Gold.

"We have to reach some agreement with the other parties about how we proceed from here. If they come up with the idea that perhaps a trip out there is worthwhile then obviously the secretary is going to consider it," State Department deputy spokesman Glyn Davies said.

Clinton said he would speak to Christopher later in the day to discuss whether it would be helpful to send a U.S. delegation to the region. "We are prepared to do anything we can that will be of assistance," he said.
Burns said the United States "is not going to point the finger of blame at either side" because it would not be helpful. But he said: "We do have private views and we are asserting those views."
Other U.S. officials, asked if Washington had asked Israel to close the tunnel, declined to comment.

Burns said Christopher did not know in advance about the opening of the tunnel but could not say if U.S. diplomats in the region knew about it. He declined to get into the merits of the dispute but said: "The fact is the tunnel was opened and the fact is there's been terrible violence since then."
He called King Hussein of Jordan's proposal to close the tunnel and have experts study the matter "a good faith effort" but said there was no U.S. view one way or the other on it.
Christopher was to meet the foreign ministers of Egypt, Israel, Saudi Arabia and the Gulf Cooperation Council states on Friday in New York.
